output.initial_context:
RELEVANT CHARACTER BACKGROUND

Adriano Santos grew up in working-class Rio de Janeiro, steeped in samba culture. He began as a child banging on tin cans and later spent two decades as a percussionist and theater technician, developing expert knowledge of drum mechanics and stage equipment. His hands know the weight of a mallet, the tension of a drum skin, and the precise angle of a spotlight. He was never famous but was known locally for fixing broken pedals and keeping time even when a band was falling apart.

Two years ago, a factory accident—a side job taken to supplement unstable theater income—caused significant partial hearing loss in his left ear and a substantial portion in his right. The doctor described it as a shotgun blast of sound, a hydraulic press slamming near his head. Now the world is muffled and he often misreads conversations. He retired early on disability but does not sit still. Every weekday morning he works in his garage, repairing old drum kits. He lives alone in the two-bedroom house his father left him, with a rusted gate. Neighbors know him as the quiet guy who plays with drums but never plays music anymore.

His tool-of-trade is precision. He lists repaired kits on a classifieds site with meticulous detail—measurements, wood grain notes, honest descriptions of scratches and wobbles. He is not sentimental about instruments; he treats them as machines to be calibrated. In the evenings he runs a YouTube channel that fact-checks popular Brazilian telenovela plots. He dismantles scenes of gunshot survival and anachronistic phones with a deadpan expression and flat voice, speaking louder than necessary because he hears himself differently. He writes long comment replies, not only on his own channel but on others, explaining why he refuses to join arts advocacy groups. He believes such groups are all talk, do not understand actual craft, and direct funding to bureaucrats rather than to broken drummers like him. He has seen grants, galas, and self-congratulatory speeches. His skepticism is a controlled bitterness that he has turned into a tool. He values precision, truth, and the concrete over the abstract. He trusts the feel of a drum skin, the smell of wood glue, and the undeniable logic of a plot hole. His channel is his way of asserting that he still counts, that his damaged ears did not take his ability to hear falsehoods.

He grew up in community but refuses to join organized groups because he believes they dilute authentic experience. He is proud of his manual skill but struggles with being defined by his disability. He has built a solitary world of repair and critique, a way to remain useful without depending on anyone. His contrarian nature is a shield, but also a means of finding clarity in a world he perceives as noisy and false.

His exchange with past buyers has been transactional: mostly young studio musicians who expect quick inspections, and he offers drum specs but no small talk. Mid-repair, he has often told visitors to wait until the glue sets; twice a buyer left and never came back. He has also paused work at a safe point to show a kit, because he hates turning away a serious buyer. He always cleans his hands before handling a drum shell, even if it costs a minute.

OBJECTIVE SITUATION

Adriano is in his garage, re-skinning a tom that has a cracked lug. He hears a knock and finds a young man at the rusted gate, holding up his phone to show the listing for the vintage Ludwig kit Adriano posted two days ago. The man says he is on his way to a studio rehearsal and can only look now—if it's not right, he'll leave. He asks Adriano to pause his work for ten minutes. Adriano's hands are coated in glue, and the tom is half-assembled. He has to decide whether to wipe off his hands and show the kit right now, or tell the man to come back tomorrow.

PRE-APPRAISAL STATE AND ACCESSIBLE MEMORIES

His fingers are tacky with glue; the tom's head is half-tensioned and needs constant monitoring. He has a faint headache from the fumes and hasn't eaten since breakfast. The Ludwig kit stands wrapped in a tarp near the door, already photographed and described in his listing.

The buyer's phone screen showing the listing's main photo reminds him of the afternoon he spent measuring the Ludwig's bearing edges. The knock on the rusted gate echoes the factory alarm that preceded the accident, but he quickly shakes it off. He remembers a previous buyer who rushed a decision and later returned the kit, haggling over a scratch Adriano had already described. He also remembers times he told mid-repair visitors to wait until glue set, and two such buyers left and never came back. He has also paused work at a safe point to show a kit because he hates turning away a serious buyer. He always cleans his hands before handling a drum shell, even if it costs a minute.
